Now the money coming in. 160 samosas at 5 rupees each: 160 times 5 is 800 rupees. That is the money earned.
He earned more than he spent, so it is a profit. 800 minus 600 is 200 rupees.
Now the percentage. We compare that 200 rupees of profit with which amount?

ask.ifNot: The question asks for the percentage on his investment, the money he put in. That is the 600 rupees he spent.

beats.say: So write the profit over the cost: 200 over 600. Both numbers divide by 200, so that fraction is one third.
one third of 100 per cent is 33 and a third per cent. Ravi makes a profit of 33 and a third per cent.
Check: one third of 600 is 200, and 200 rupees is exactly his profit.
So for a profit percentage: find the profit, put it over the cost, and turn that fraction into a percentage.
Deepa spends 400 rupees on materials and makes 50 rakhis to sell at 12 rupees each. At the end of the day, 10 rakhis are unsold. What percentage profit does she make on the money she spent?
Here is the plan. Add up the money going out, add up the money coming in, and the gap between them is the profit.
The money going out is quick this time. Deepa spent 400 rupees on materials, and that is the whole cost.
Deepa made 50 rakhis. But how many were actually sold?

ask.ifNot: Look at the story again: 10 rakhis stayed unsold. They bring in no money, so they come off. 50 minus 10 is 40.

beats.say: That leaves 40 rakhis sold. Careful here: the 10 that stayed unsold earn nothing, but they still cost money.
Now the money coming in. 40 rakhis at 12 rupees each: 40 times 12 is 480 rupees. That is all the money earned.
Now subtract. 480 minus 400 is 80. That is the profit.
Now the percentage. We compare that 80 rupees of profit with which amount?

ask.ifNot: The question asks for the percentage on her investment, the money she put in. That is the 400 rupees she spent.

beats.say: So write the profit over the cost: 80 over 400. Divide the top and the bottom by 80, and that fraction is one fifth.
one fifth of 100 per cent is 20 per cent. Deepa makes a profit of 20 per cent.
Check: 20 per cent of 400 is 80, and 80 rupees is exactly her profit.
So the method is: find the profit in rupees, compare it with the money spent, and write that as a percentage.

Kavya spends 600 rupees on ingredients and 150 rupees on stall rent. She sells 50 cups of chai at 12 rupees each and 40 samosa plates at 15 rupees each. Then she donates 20 per cent of her profit. How much of the profit is left?
Profit is the money that comes in, take away the money that goes out. So we need two totals: what Kavya spent, and what she earned.
Start with the money going out: the ingredients and the stall rent. 600 plus 150 is 750 rupees, and that is everything Kavya spent.
Now the money coming in. 50 cups of chai at 12 rupees each: 50 times 12 is 600 rupees.
Then 40 samosa plates at 15 rupees each: 40 times 15 is 600 rupees.
Altogether, 600 plus 600 is 1,200 rupees earned.
Now subtract. 1,200 minus 750 is 450. That is the profit.
Now the donation: 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of which amount?

ask.ifNot: The story says 20 per cent of her profit. So the donation is worked out on the 450 rupees, not on everything she earned.

beats.say: 10 per cent is one tenth, so 10 per cent of 450 is 45.
20 per cent is double that. So 90 rupees go to the school.
Take the donation away from the profit. 450 minus 90 is 360, so Kavya has 360 rupees left.
Check: what she kept and what she gave should make the whole profit. 360 plus 90 is 450. It fits.
So the method is: find the profit first, then take the percentage of exactly the amount the story names.

Meera spends 240 rupees on ingredients and 60 rupees on paper plates. She makes 60 samosas and sells each one for 8 rupees. Then she gives 25 per cent of her profit to charity. How much does she donate?

board.text: Costs ₹240 + ₹60; 60 samosas at ₹8; gives 25% of profit

beats.say: To find a profit we need two amounts: the money Meera spent, and the money she earned. Profit is earned, take away spent.
Start with the money going out: the ingredients and the paper plates. 240 plus 60 is 300 rupees, and that is everything Meera spent.
Now the money coming in. 60 samosas at 8 rupees each: 60 times 8 is 480 rupees. That is all the money earned.
Last step: 480 minus 300 is 180. That is the profit.
Now the donation: 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of which amount?

ask.ifNot: The story says 25 per cent of her profit. So the donation is worked out on the 180 rupees, not on everything she earned.

beats.say: 25 per cent is the same as one quarter. So we need a quarter of the profit, and that means dividing by 4.
180 divided by 4 is 45. Meera donates 45 rupees.
Check: 4 quarters make the whole. 45 times 4 is 180, and that is the profit.
So the method is: find the profit first, then take the percentage of exactly the amount the story names.

Meera spends 400 rupees on ingredients and 100 rupees on packaging. She makes 100 samosas and sells 80 per cent of them at 8 rupees each. Then she spends 25 per cent of her profit on a maths book. What does the book cost?

board.text: Costs ₹400 + ₹100; 80% of 100 at ₹8; book 25% of profit

beats.say: Here is the plan. Add up the money going out, add up the money coming in, and the gap between them is the profit.
Start with the money going out: the ingredients and the packaging. 400 plus 100 is 500 rupees, and that is everything Meera spent.
She made 100 samosas and sold 80 per cent of them. How many is that?

ask.ifNot: Per cent means out of 100. She made exactly 100 samosas, so 80 per cent of them is 80 samosas.

beats.say: 80 per cent of 100 is 80. The other 20 were given away, so they bring in nothing.
Now the money coming in. 80 samosas at 8 rupees each: 80 times 8 is 640 rupees. That is all the money earned.
Money earned, take away money spent: 640 minus 500 is 140. That is the profit.
The book costs 25 per cent of the profit. 25 per cent is one quarter, so we divide the profit by 4.
140 divided by 4 is 35. The maths book costs 35 rupees.
Here is the trap: taking a quarter of the 640 rupees she earned. The story says a quarter of the profit, and the profit is much smaller.
Check: 4 quarters make the whole. 35 times 4 is 140, and that is the profit.
So work in order: the cost, the sales, the profit, and only then the percentage. And always ask: a percentage of which amount?
Vikram buys ingredients for 250 rupees and sells samosas worth 350 rupees in total. He donates 20 per cent of his profit to a charity for planting trees. How much does he donate?

board.text: Spent ₹250, sold for ₹350; gives 20% of profit

beats.say: First we need the profit: money earned, take away money spent. 350 minus 250 is 100 rupees.
Now the donation: 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of which amount?

ask.ifNot: The story says 20 per cent of his profit. So the donation is worked out on the 100 rupees, not on the 350 rupees he took in.

beats.say: Per cent means out of every 100. And his profit is exactly 100 rupees, which makes this a friendly one.
20 per cent of 100 is 20. Vikram donates 20 rupees.
Here is the trap. 20 per cent of the 350 rupees he earned would be 70 rupees, and that is one of the choices. But the gift comes out of the profit.
Check that it makes sense: 100 minus 20 leaves him 80 rupees of profit. He gives the small share and keeps the big one.
So work in order: the cost, the sales, the profit, and only then the percentage. And always ask: a percentage of which amount?

Sneha spends 750 rupees on tea leaves, sugar and milk. She sells 150 cups of chai at 8 rupees each, then gives 10 per cent of her total earnings to the school. How much profit is left after the donation?

board.text: Spent ₹750; 150 cups at ₹8 each; gives 10% of earnings

beats.say: To find a profit we need two amounts: the money Sneha spent, and the money she earned. Profit is earned, take away spent.
The money going out is quick this time. Sneha spent 750 rupees on tea leaves, sugar and milk, and that is the whole cost.
Now the money coming in. 150 cups at 8 rupees each: 150 times 8 is 1,200 rupees. That is the money earned.
Now the donation: 10 per cent. But 10 per cent of which amount?

ask.ifNot: Read that line once more: 10 per cent of her total earnings. Earnings means all the money that came in, the 1,200 rupees.

beats.say: 10 per cent is one tenth, so we divide by 10. 1,200 divided by 10 is 120 rupees for the school.
After the donation she has 1,200 minus 120, which is 1,080 rupees.
Now take away what she spent. 1,080 minus 750 is 330. Sneha has 330 rupees of profit left.
Careful: in this story the donation comes out of the earnings, not out of the profit. Always read which amount the percentage belongs to.
Check: profit, donation and cost together should use up all she earned. 330 plus 120 plus 750 is 1,200. It fits.
So the method is: find the profit first, then take the percentage of exactly the amount the story names.

Priya's father buys diyas at 3 rupees each, and spends 200 rupees on paints and 100 on glitter. He sells 80 per cent at 12 rupees and 20 per cent at 7 rupees, and makes 500 rupees profit. How many diyas did he buy?
We don't know how many diyas there are, so let's watch a small group of 10. Out of every 10 diyas, 8 sell at the full price and 2 at the lower price.
The 8 diyas at 12 rupees each bring in 96 rupees.
The 2 diyas at 7 rupees each bring in 14 rupees.
Together, 96 plus 14 is 110 rupees coming in from every 10 diyas.
But those 10 diyas cost 3 rupees each to buy. 10 times 3 is 30 rupees.
So every group of 10 diyas leaves him 110 minus 30, which is 80 rupees.
That 80 rupees from each group has two jobs to do. What must all the groups add up to?

ask.ifNot: Before there is any profit, the paints and glitter must be paid for. That is 300 rupees, and then the 500 rupees of profit comes on top.

beats.say: Paints, glitter and profit: 200 plus 100 plus 500 is 800 rupees to be covered.
Each group gives 80 rupees. 800 divided by 80 is 10, so he needs 10 groups.
10 groups of 10 diyas is 100 diyas. That is how many he bought.
Check with 100 diyas. 80 of them sell at 12 rupees and 20 at 7 rupees. That is 960 plus 140, which is 1,100 rupees.
The cost is 100 times 3, plus the 300 for paints and glitter, so 600 rupees. And 1,100 minus 600 is 500, the profit in the story.
So when the number of things is hidden, find what one small group leaves you. Then see how many groups cover the extra costs and the profit.

Priya's father buys diyas at 3 rupees each. He spends 400 rupees on paints, 200 on glitter and 300 on a tempo. He sells every diya at 8 rupees and makes a profit of 600 rupees. How many diyas did he buy?
We don't know how many diyas there are, so start with just one. He buys it for 3 rupees and sells it for 8, so each diya leaves him 5 rupees.
Now the extra costs: the paints, the glitter and the tempo. 400 plus 200 plus 300 is 900 rupees.
Those 5 rupees from each diya have to add up to how much?

ask.ifNot: The 5 rupees from each diya must first pay back the 900 rupees of extras. Only after that does the 600 rupees of profit appear. So they cover both.

beats.say: So the diyas must bring in 900 plus 600, which is 1,500 rupees, 5 rupees at a time.
How many 5s make 1,500? 1,500 divided by 5 is 300. He bought 300 diyas.
The slip here is dividing only the 600 rupees of profit by 5. That forgets the paints, the glitter and the tempo, which the diyas have to pay for first.
Check with 300 diyas. Selling them brings in 300 times 8, which is 2,400 rupees.
Buying them costs 300 times 3, which is 900, plus 900 of extras: 1,800 rupees. And 2,400 minus 1,800 is 600, the profit in the story.
So when the number of things is hidden, find what one of them leaves you. Then see how many it takes to cover the extra costs and the profit.

Deepa sells all her marigold garlands, and 60 of her 80 rose garlands at 40 rupees each. The other 20 rose garlands are donated. If she had sold those 20 as well, how much more profit would she have made?

board.text: 80 rose garlands bought at ₹25; 60 sold at ₹40, 20 unsold

beats.say: This story is full of numbers, and we could work out two whole profits. There is a quicker way: compare the real day with the imagined day, where every rose garland sells.
Between the two days, which amount changes?

choices: what she paid for the garlands
ask.ifNot: She bought the same garlands on both days, and sold the same marigolds. The only difference is whether those last 20 rose garlands bring in money.

beats.say: She paid for all 80 rose garlands either way, so the cost does not move. The ribbons, the transport and the marigolds stay the same too.
So the only extra is 20 more garlands sold at 40 rupees each. 20 times 40 is 800. She would have made 800 rupees more.
It is tempting to take the 25 rupees cost off each of those garlands. But that money was already spent on both days, so it does not change the gap.
Check with the rose sales. On the imagined day, 80 times 40 is 3,200 rupees. On the real day, 60 times 40 is 2,400 rupees.
3,200 minus 2,400 is 800. The same answer, and everything else in the story cancels out.
So when a question asks how much more, look for the one thing that changes. Everything that stays the same can be left alone.

Kabir's mom buys 50 samosa plates at 24 rupees each and pays 100 rupees stall rent. She sells 35 plates at a profit of 25 per cent, and the other 15 at 10 per cent below the cost price. Does she make a profit or a loss overall?
Here is the plan. Add up the money going out, add up the money coming in, and the gap between them is the profit.
Start with the money going out. The plates: 50 times 24 is 1,200 rupees.
Now add the stall rent. 1,200 plus 100 is 1,300 rupees. That is everything Kabir's mom spent.
35 plates sell at a profit of 25 per cent. But 25 per cent of what?

choices: of ₹24, the cost of a plate
ask.ifNot: A profit percentage is always counted on the cost price. Each plate cost 24 rupees, so the profit on one plate is 25 per cent of 24.

beats.say: 25 per cent is one quarter, and a quarter of 24 is 6. So each of these plates sells for 24 plus 6, which is 30 rupees.
Now the money coming in. 35 plates at 30 rupees each: 35 times 30 is 1,050 rupees.
The other 15 plates sell below cost. 10 per cent of 24 is not a whole number of rupees, so let's take all 15 plates together.
Those 15 plates cost 15 times 24, which is 360 rupees.
10 per cent is one tenth, so 10 per cent of 360 is 36. She gets 360 minus 36, which is 324 rupees for those plates.
Altogether, 1,050 plus 324 is 1,374 rupees earned.
Now subtract. 1,374 minus 1,300 is 74. Kabir's mom makes a profit of 74 rupees.
Did you notice the rent? Leave it out and the profit looks 100 rupees bigger. The rent is money spent, so it belongs in the cost.
Let's check. The profit and the cost together should make the money earned: 74 plus 1,300 is 1,374. It fits.
So with percentages: turn each one into rupees first, using the cost price. Then it is the usual plan: earned, take away spent.

Meera buys 40 boxes of sparklers at 75 rupees each. She sells 30 boxes at a profit of 20 per cent, and the other 10 boxes at 10 per cent below her cost price. What is her profit or loss on all 40 boxes?
Here is the plan. Add up the money going out, add up the money coming in, and the gap between them is the profit.
Start with the money going out. The boxes: 40 times 75 is 3,000 rupees. That is everything Meera spent.
30 boxes sell at a profit of 20 per cent. But 20 per cent of what?

choices: of ₹75, the cost of a box
ask.ifNot: A profit percentage is always counted on the cost price. Each box cost 75 rupees, so the profit on one box is 20 per cent of 75.

beats.say: 20 per cent is one fifth, and 75 divided by 5 is 15. So each of these boxes sells for 75 plus 15, which is 90 rupees.
Now the money coming in. 30 boxes at 90 rupees each: 30 times 90 is 2,700 rupees.
The 10 damp boxes sell below cost. Take them all together: they cost 10 times 75, which is 750 rupees.
10 per cent is one tenth, so 10 per cent of 750 is 75. She gets 750 minus 75, which is 675 rupees for those boxes.
Altogether, 2,700 plus 675 is 3,375 rupees earned.
Money earned, take away money spent: 3,375 minus 3,000 is 375. That is a profit of 375 rupees.
Two different percentages, and both are counted on the cost price. One goes up from the cost, and the other comes down from it.
Let's check. The profit and the cost together should make the money earned: 375 plus 3,000 is 3,375. It fits.
So with percentages: turn each one into rupees first, using the cost price. Then it is the usual plan: earned, take away spent.

Vikram spends 450 rupees on tea leaves, 150 on milk and 100 on sugar. He makes 140 cups of chai at 10 rupees a cup. 15 teachers each buy one cup at a 20 per cent discount, and the rest sell at full price.
Here is the plan. Add up the money going out, add up the money coming in, and the gap between them is the profit.
Start with the money going out: the tea leaves, the milk and the sugar. 450 plus 150 plus 100 is 700 rupees, and that is everything Vikram spent.
A teacher gets 20 per cent off a cup that costs 10 rupees. What does the teacher pay?

ask.ifNot: 20 per cent of 10 rupees is 2 rupees. That is the discount, the part taken off. So the teacher pays 10 minus 2, which is 8 rupees.

beats.say: 20 per cent of 10 is 2, so 2 rupees come off. The 2 is the discount, not the price: a teacher pays 8 rupees.
Now the money coming in. 15 teachers' cups at 8 rupees each: 15 times 8 is 120 rupees.
The other cups go at full price. 140 minus 15 leaves 125 cups.
Next, 125 cups at the full 10 rupees: 125 times 10 is 1,250 rupees.
Put the sales together: 120 plus 1,250 is 1,370 rupees. That is the money earned.
Money earned, take away money spent: 1,370 minus 700 is 670. That is a profit of 670 rupees.
Let's check. The profit and the cost together should make the money earned: 670 plus 700 is 1,370. It fits.
So the method is: total cost, then the money from each batch, then earned take away spent.
Ravi's father buys tea supplies for 1,500 rupees and pays 300 rupees stall rent. He sells 120 cups of chai at 15 rupees each. Then he takes 20 per cent off the price and sells the last 80 cups.

board.text: Supplies ₹1,500, rent ₹300; 120 cups at ₹15; 80 at 20% off

beats.say: Here is the plan. Add up the money going out, add up the money coming in, and the gap between them is the profit.
Start with the money going out: the tea supplies and the stall rent. 1,500 plus 300 is 1,800 rupees, and that is everything Ravi's father spent.
Now the money coming in. 120 cups at the full price of 15 rupees: 120 times 15 is 1,800 rupees.
For the second half, 20 per cent comes off the 15 rupee price. What is the new price?

ask.ifNot: 20 per cent is one fifth, and one fifth of 15 is 3. That 3 rupees is the discount. The new price is 15 minus 3, which is 12 rupees.

beats.say: One fifth of 15 is 3, so 3 rupees come off. The 3 is the discount, not the price: each cup now sells for 12 rupees.
Next, 80 cups at the lower price of 12 rupees: 80 times 12 is 960 rupees.
Put the sales together: 1,800 plus 960 is 2,760 rupees. That is the money earned.
Last step: 2,760 minus 1,800 is 960. So the profit is 960 rupees.
One more thing to watch: the rent is paid after the match, but it is still a cost of the day. Leave it out and the profit looks 300 rupees too big.
Let's check. The profit and the cost together should make the money earned: 960 plus 1,800 is 2,760. It fits.
So the method is: total cost, then the money from each batch, then earned take away spent.

Priya's family buys 200 diyas at 3 rupees each, and spends 250 rupees on paint and 350 on wax and wicks. They sell 3 quarters of the diyas at 12 rupees each, and the rest at 25 per cent off that price.
Here is the plan. Add up the money going out, add up the money coming in, and the gap between them is the profit.
Start with the money going out. The diyas: 200 times 3 is 600 rupees.
Now add the paint and glitter and the wax and wicks. 600 plus 250 plus 350 is 1,200 rupees. That is everything Priya's family spent.
3 quarters of the 200 diyas sell at the full price. How many diyas is that?

ask.ifNot: One quarter of 200 is 200 divided by 4, which is 50. So 3 quarters is 3 times 50, and that is 150 diyas.

beats.say: A quarter of 200 is 50, so 3 quarters is 150 diyas. The last quarter, 50 diyas, gets the discount.
Now the money coming in. 150 diyas at 12 rupees each: 150 times 12 is 1,800 rupees.
25 per cent off means a quarter of the price comes off. A quarter of 12 is 3, so the discount price is 12 minus 3, which is 9 rupees.
Then 50 diyas at the discount price of 9 rupees: 50 times 9 is 450 rupees.
Altogether, 1,800 plus 450 is 2,250 rupees earned.
Last step: 2,250 minus 1,200 is 1,050. Priya's family makes a profit of 1,050 rupees.
Check by adding back. 1,050 plus 1,200 is 2,250, exactly the money that came in.
So when things sell at two prices: work out each batch on its own, add the two, then take away the total cost.
Meera's father buys 80 sugarcanes at 10 rupees each, and spends 240 rupees on ice, cups and lemon. Every 2 sugarcanes fill 5 glasses, and he sells each glass for 15 rupees. What is his profit?

board.text: 80 canes at ₹10, extras ₹240; 2 canes fill 5 glasses at ₹15

beats.say: Profit is the money that comes in, take away the money that goes out. So we need two totals: what Meera's father spent, and what he earned.
Start with the money going out. The sugarcanes: 80 times 10 is 800 rupees.
Now add the ice, cups and lemon. 800 plus 240 is 1,040 rupees. That is everything Meera's father spent.
He sells glasses, not sugarcanes. Every 2 sugarcanes fill 5 glasses. How do we find the glasses from 80 sugarcanes?

ask.ifNot: The sugarcanes go into the machine 2 at a time. So first count the pairs, 80 divided by 2, and then each pair gives 5 glasses.

beats.say: 80 divided by 2 is 40 pairs of sugarcanes.
Each pair fills 5 glasses, so 40 times 5 is 200 glasses.
Now the money coming in. 200 glasses at 15 rupees each: 200 times 15 is 3,000 rupees. That is all the money earned.
Last step: 3,000 minus 1,040 is 1,960. So the profit is 1,960 rupees.
The slip to avoid is selling 80 glasses, one for each sugarcane. The story sells glasses, so the sugarcanes had to be turned into glasses first.
Check by adding back. 1,960 plus 1,040 is 3,000, exactly the money that came in.
So the method is: total cost first, total sales next, and profit is sales take away cost.

Priya's father buys 5 boxes of chikki at 360 rupees a box, with 24 bars in each box, and pays 200 rupees for transport. 12 bars get crushed, and he sells the rest at 25 rupees each. What is his profit from this sale?

board.text: 5 boxes at ₹360, 24 bars each; transport ₹200; 12 crushed

beats.say: Here is the plan. Add up the money going out, add up the money coming in, and the gap between them is the profit.
Start with the money going out. The boxes: 5 times 360 is 1,800 rupees.
Now add the transport. 1,800 plus 200 is 2,000 rupees. That is everything Priya's father spent.
He buys boxes, but he sells bars. So how many bars are there? 5 boxes of 24 bars: 5 times 24 is 120 bars.
He had 120 bars. But how many were actually sold?

ask.ifNot: Look at the story again: 12 bars were crushed. They bring in no money, so they come off. 120 minus 12 is 108.

beats.say: 120 minus 12 is 108, so 108 bars were sold. The cost does not shrink, though: all 120 were paid for.
Now the money coming in. 108 bars at 25 rupees each: 108 times 25 is 2,700 rupees. That is the money earned.
The story adds that he later spends 180 rupees on packaging for the next order. Does that come off this profit?

choices: No, it belongs to the next order
ask.ifNot: The question asks for the profit from this sale, before the packaging is counted. That 180 rupees is a cost of the next order, so we leave it out.

beats.say: Money earned, take away money spent: 2,700 minus 2,000 is 700. So the profit is 700 rupees.
A quick check: 700 plus 2,000 is 2,700, and that is the money earned. It works.
So in a story like this: all the costs count, but only the things really sold bring money in. Then subtract.
Kavya's class spends 600 rupees on ingredients and makes 200 samosas to sell at 8 rupees each. They sell 90 per cent of the samosas and give the rest away. What is their profit?
To find a profit we need two amounts: the money Kavya's class spent, and the money they earned. Profit is earned, take away spent.
The money going out is quick this time. Kavya's class spent 600 rupees on ingredients, and that is the whole cost.
They sold 90 per cent of the 200 samosas. How many samosas is that?

ask.ifNot: 10 per cent of 200 is 20. And 90 per cent is 9 lots of that, so 9 times 20, which is 180 samosas.

beats.say: 10 per cent of 200 is 20 samosas. So 90 per cent is 9 times as many, and that is 180 samosas sold.
Now the money coming in. 180 samosas at 8 rupees each: 180 times 8 is 1,440 rupees. That is the money earned.
Money earned, take away money spent: 1,440 minus 600 is 840. Kavya's class makes a profit of 840 rupees.
Did you spot the trap? Selling all 200 would bring in more money, but 20 samosas were given away and earned nothing.
Let's check. The profit and the cost together should make the money earned: 840 plus 600 is 1,440. It fits.
So the method is: total up every cost, count only what was really sold, then take the cost away from the money earned.
Ravi buys cricket balls for 45 rupees each and sells them for 63 rupees each. During the season he sells 20 balls. What is his total profit?

board.text: Buys at ₹45, sells at ₹63; 20 balls sold

beats.say: Every ball costs the same and sells for the same. So we can find the profit on just one ball first.
Selling price, take away cost price: 63 minus 45 is 18. Each ball earns Ravi 18 rupees.
That is one ball. What do we do for all 20 balls?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 20 balls earns the same 18 rupees. 20 lots of 18 means we multiply.

beats.say: 18 times 20 is 360. The total profit is 360 rupees.
Careful with 63 times 20. That is all the money that came in, not the profit, because every ball cost money too.
Check the long way. Ravi took in 20 times 63, which is 1,260 rupees, and spent 20 times 45, which is 900 rupees.
1,260 minus 900 is 360. Both ways agree.
So when every item has the same cost and the same price, find the profit on one, then multiply by how many were sold.
Meena's mother spends 8 rupees on ingredients for each samosa, and sells each one for 12 rupees. She makes and sells 25 samosas. What is her total profit?

board.text: Each samosa costs ₹8, sells for ₹12; 25 sold

beats.say: Every samosa costs the same and sells for the same. So we can find the profit on just one samosa first.
Selling price, take away cost price: 12 minus 8 is 4. Each samosa earns Meena's mother 4 rupees.
That is one samosa. What do we do for all 25 samosas?

ask.ifNot: Each of the 25 samosas earns the same 4 rupees. 25 lots of 4 means we multiply.

beats.say: 4 times 25 is 100. The total profit is 100 rupees.
Careful with 12 times 25. That is all the money that came in, not the profit, because every samosa cost money too.
Check the long way. Meena's mother took in 25 times 12, which is 300 rupees, and spent 25 times 8, which is 200 rupees.

So when every item has the same cost and the same price, find the profit on one, then multiply by how many were sold.
Ananya buys packets of chai masala for 35 rupees each, and ties a ribbon that costs 5 rupees on each one. She sells them for 56 rupees each, and sells 12 packets. What is her total profit?

board.text: Packet ₹35 + ribbon ₹5; sells at ₹56; 12 packets sold

beats.say: Every packet costs the same and sells for the same. So we can find the profit on just one packet first.
What does one finished packet really cost Ananya?

ask.ifNot: She pays 35 rupees for the packet, and then 5 rupees more for its ribbon. Both are money spent on that one packet.

beats.say: The packet and its ribbon together: 35 plus 5 is 40 rupees. Leaving out the ribbon is the trap in this story.
Selling price, take away cost: 56 minus 40 is 16. Each packet earns her 16 rupees.
She sells 12 packets, so we multiply. 12 times 16 is 192. Ananya's total profit is 192 rupees.
Check the long way. She took in 12 times 56, which is 672 rupees, and spent 12 times 40, which is 480 rupees.
672 minus 480 is 192. Both ways agree.
So when every item has the same cost and the same price, find the full cost of one, then the profit on one, then multiply.
